newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada's Martin to announce pension plan deal.
newsitem.headline: Canada's Martin to announce pension plan deal.

text.p: Canadian Finance Minister Paul Martin will announce changes to the Canada Pension Plan (CPP) on Friday, apparently to safeguard its future as the baby boom generation ages.
Martin's office said he would introduce into Parliament draft legislation on changes to the plan at about 1210 EST (1710 GMT), with a news conference to follow.

The federal government has been working with the provinces to figure out a way to bring more money into the plan to make sure it is viable when the baby boomers start retiring, and now appeared to have struck a deal.

The Toronto newspaper said the CPP changes were generally along the lines tentatively worked out last fall, under which CPP contribution rates will rise over the next eight years to 10 percent from their current level of 5.85 percent on the first C$35,400 of income.
The tax is split evenly between employee and employer.

The idea is to move tax rates higher while the baby boomers are still working and hopefully to cap the rate at 10 percent. If speedy action were not taken, the chief actuary of the CPP warned, rates would have to rise to 14.2 percent by 2030.
The Globe said a 10-cent cut in UI premiums would cost Martin C$650 million. It pointed out that he had already made a budgetary planning assumption of a five-cent cut. ((Randall

The Globe and Mail newspaper reported on Friday that Ontario, Canada's most populous province, agreed to back the CPP reform, giving Martin the requisite two-thirds of the provinces representing at least two-thirds of the population.
The Globe said Martin gave ground on Ontario's demand that Ottawa accompany CPP rate increases with cuts to unemployment insurance (UI) premiums.
It said that in Tuesday's federal budget for 1997-98, Martin would announce a small cut in UI premiums -- to $2.80 per $100 of insurable earnings from $2.90 -- to take effect next year.
